keep: The idea is named up front: an eigenvector is an arrow a matrix only stretches, Av = λv, its eigenvalue is the stretch, and the numbers come first from det(A − λI) = 0, then the directions from (A − λI)v = 0.

The picture is the brief's stretch finder: a probe v swept round, Av beside it, the line lighting with λ when Av lands on v's line, presets stretch, mirror, shear and quarter turn, and a λ slider whose A − λI grid goes flat with determinant 0 at each eigenvalue, the crushed line dashed on the lit line.

One worked example runs from the rule: A = [3 1; 0 2] read as a mix of columns gives (1, 0) with 3 and (−1, 1) with 2, then (3 − λ)(2 − λ) = 0 finds the same two; B = [2 −1; −1 2] gives λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0, 1 with (1, 1) and 3 with (1, −1), checked by multiplying; C = [1 1 0; 1 2 1; 0 1 1] in practice gives 0, 1 and 3, the 0 line being lesson 4's null space.

The causal step is given: (A − λI)v = 0 with v nonzero means A − λI crushes something, which happens only when it flattens, so its area scale, the determinant, is 0. The trace and determinant checks are derived from (λ − p)(λ − q), not just stated.

The brief's misconceptions each get a screen: multiples (2), no eigenvector for a quarter turn and one for a shear (4), λI not λ (6), one eigenvalue known (8), v = 0 as a slip (10), pairs matched (13); the diagonal misread is a mixed puzzle (12) and a common mistake.

Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with two mixed puzzles (12, 13). Three footnotes, each on a definition or rule he might look up, none named in the text. The common-mode choke is a new analogy from his trade with the same [a b; b a] shape as B.
fix: False absolute: 'Most arrows get knocked off their own line by a matrix' fails for I or 2I, which knock off none. Say a matrix usually does.
False absolute in practice: 'Complex roots mean no real line stays put' fails for a 3 by 3 with one real root. Limit it to a 2 by 2.
False absolute in practice: 'one row is enough' fails when that row is all zeros, as in [0 0; 1 1]. Say one nonzero row.
Causal step skipped for the quarter turn: 'moves every arrow off its line' gives the effect only. Say it turns each arrow 90°, so Av is square to v.
Link to lesson 4 missing: (A − λI)v = 0 is the null space of A − λI. Name it with lesson 4's term.
